raw_case_text:
A forty-two-year-old female PLHIV (people living with HIV) not on antiretroviral treatment (ART) was admitted with the history of sudden onset left hemiplegia and altered sensorium for 4 days. There was no history of fever, headache, vomiting or convulsion. She received antituberculosis treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 6 months back. On examination she was afebrile, pulse was 54 per minute regular and blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg. Pallor and oral candidiasis were noted. There was no evidence of lymphadenopathy.
Central nervous system examination revealed GCS of 5/15. Right pupil was dilated and nonreacting, no papilledema on fundoscopy. Left upper motor neuron facial palsy present. Patient had left hemiplegia. Other systems examination was normal.
On investigations, her hemoglobin was 9 gm%, total leucocytic count was 8000/cumm. Metabolic lab was normal. Her CD4 count was 14/cumm and chest X-ray was normal. CT scan brain showed large 5x4x4.5 cm abscess in right frontoparietal region with severe mass effect and leptomeningitis. [Figure 1]. Urgent drainage of intracranial abscess was done by neurosurgeon. Approximately 50 cc pus was drained.
Patient became ambulatory by fifth postoperative day with marked improvement in sensorium.
Acid fast bacilli were seen on ZN staining of pus. Pus was inoculated on Lowenstein Jensen's medium. Single white colony was grown by second week which was not rough and dry as seen in typical myocobacterium tuberculosis growth, but was smooth and wet in appearance and nonpigmented. Smear was strongly positive for acid-fast bacilli which were long and slender. Further confirmation was done by niacin test which was negative which favored the infection by NTM. The organism was further identified as MAI by standard biochemical tests.
Patient was started on tab Clarithromycin, tab Ethambutol, and ART. Repeat CT scan brain after 1 week, showed reduction in the size of abscess with perilesional edema [Figure 1].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old female presenting with acute onset of left hemiplegia and altered sensorium for 4 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed sudden-onset left-sided hemiplegia and progressive deterioration of sensorium over 4 days. She had no preceding history of fever, headache, vomiting, or convulsive episodes. Six months prior to admission, she completed antituberculosis treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic retroviral infection not receiving antiretroviral treatment. Pulmonary tuberculosis treated with full antituberculosis therapy completed 6 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute focal weakness (left hemiplegia), altered level of consciousness, and oral thrush; negative for fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Home medications: none. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: afebrile, pulse: 54 beats/min (regular), blood pressure: 140/90 mmHg. General: pallor and oral candidiasis; no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Neurological: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 5/15; right pupil dilated and non-reactive; fundoscopy: no papilledema; left upper motor neuron facial nerve palsy; left flaccid hemiplegia. Other systemic examinations normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 9 g/dL (9 gm%); total leukocyte count: 8,000/cumm; routine metabolic laboratory tests: normal; baseline chest radiograph: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain computed tomography (CT): large 5 x 4 x 4.5 cm abscess in the right frontoparietal region with severe mass effect and leptomeningitis. Repeat brain CT at 1 week postoperatively: reduction in abscess cavity size with residual perilesional edema.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Right frontoparietal brain abscess and leptomeningitis caused by non-tuberculous mycobacteria / Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI/MAC) complex in advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection / AIDS (CD4 count 14/cumm). Classical Mycobacterium tuberculosis ruled out by negative niacin test and colony morphology. Confirmed by Ziehl-Neelsen staining of aspirated pus demonstrating long, slender acid-fast bacilli and Lowenstein-Jensen culture yielding smooth, moist, nonpigmented white colonies at 2 weeks, identified as MAI by standard biochemical testing. Management & Outcome: Underwent emergent neurosurgical drainage of approximately 50 cc of purulent fluid, resulting in rapid neurological recovery (ambulatory with marked sensorium improvement by postoperative day 5). Initiated on oral clarithromycin, ethambutol, and combination antiretroviral therapy (cART).
